facts.text: On this date in 1963, the first episode of Doctor Who aired on BBC One — one day after JFK's assassination, an event so dominant that the premiere was largely ignored and had to be rebroadcast the following week.
On this date in 1876, the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks was founded in New York City, originally as a social club for actors trying to get around Sunday liquor laws.
Manila is the most densely populated city on Earth, packing over 70,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any neighborhood in New York, Tokyo, or Mumbai.
More people live inside a 4,000km circle centered on Bangladesh than live outside it — roughly half of all humanity fits within that single drawn boundary.
Canada is larger than the entire European Union by land area, yet its population is smaller than California's.
On this day in 1954, the Dow Jones closed at 382 — finally recovering its 1929 peak. It had taken 25 years for investors to break even.
On this day in 1963, the NYSE closed early out of respect for President Kennedy, one of only a handful of unscheduled closures in its 230-year history.
The entire US bond market is roughly twice the size of the US stock market, yet most retail investors couldn't name a single bond they own.
Berkshire Hathaway's Class A share once traded below $8. It has never split, and today trades above $700,000 — the most expensive share price of any major public company.
The Dutch East India Company paid dividends for nearly 200 consecutive years, making it arguably the most successful income investment in human history.
On this day in 1859, Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species.' The first edition sold out in a single day — his publisher had expected it to sell as well as a book on pigeons.
On this day in 1654, mathematician Blaise Pascal experienced a mystical vision so intense he sewed a written account of it into his coat lining, where it was found only after his death.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces most of its atoms every few years, yet the pattern persists. You are less a thing than a process — a wave that holds its shape while the water moves through.
Octopuses have three hearts, blue blood, and neurons distributed throughout their arms, meaning each limb can taste, feel, and act semi-independently of the brain.
On this day in 1963, the first episode of Doctor Who aired — the day after JFK was assassinated, nearly burying the debut entirely.
Oxford University was already 150 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded.
On this day in 1876, the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks was founded in New York — originally a drinking club for actors dodging Sunday liquor laws.
Woolly mammoths were still alive on Wrangel Island when the Great Pyramid was being built, outlasting the mainland extinction by 6,000 years.
Harvard University existed for 140 years before the lightning rod was invented, meaning every early building was one storm away from disaster.

Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows,' 2012. It spread so fast linguists now study it as a neologism.
Apricity (n.): the warmth of the sun in winter. From Latin 'apricus,' sun-warmed. First recorded in Henry Cockeram's English dictionary, 1623, then vanished — a perfect word lost for three centuries.

On this date in 1859, Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species,' and with it the word 'evolved' entered common use. It was the last word of the book, quietly ending a paragraph that rewrote biology.

Mamihlapinatapai: a look shared between two people who both want something but neither will initiate. From the Yaghan language of Tierra del Fuego, once listed by Guinness as the world's most succinct word.

Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh word for a longing for a home that may never have existed — nostalgia, grief, and yearning fused into one. Welsh has no direct equivalent in English, which is precisely why it escapes translation.
On this date in 2017, Bitcoin hit $8,000 for the first time — but more quietly, SegWit adoption crossed 10% of transactions that same week, a protocol shift that mattered far more than the price.
On this date in 2021, the Ethereum network processed its 1 billionth transaction, a milestone reached faster than any prior blockchain by an order of magnitude.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named by Satoshi Nakamoto — the community coined the term in a 2010 BitcoinTalk thread, and Nakamoto never used it in any known communication.
The DAO hack of 2016 didn't exploit a bug in Ethereum — it exploited code that worked exactly as written. The attacker used a legal reentrancy call; the 'bug' was in the developer's mental model.

Ethereum validators don't confirm transactions — they propose and attest to blocks. The distinction matters: over two-thirds of attestations must agree before a block achieves finality, a quorum no single entity controls.
On this date in 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. It reached 1 million users in 5 days — faster than any consumer product in history — without a single dollar spent on advertising.
On this date in 2023, the EU AI Act cleared its final major political hurdle. It's the first binding AI law by any major economy, and it classifies general-purpose AI above 10²⁵ FLOPs as high-risk.
AlphaFold 2 predicted protein structures for nearly every known protein — ~200 million — in under a year. Structural biologists had manually solved roughly 170,000 structures across five decades.
GPT-4 was trained on an estimated ~2×10²⁵ FLOPs. The human brain runs on roughly 20 watts. Matching its training cost in energy would power that brain for about 500,000 years.
The first neural network to beat humans at Go, AlphaGo, did so in 2016. Its successor AlphaZero learned Go from scratch — no human games — and surpassed AlphaGo in 72 hours.
